title: Three founders, eight directors, and the Intel chairmanship overhang
body:
## The founding axis

Jitendra Mohan spent the first two decades of his career doing what the best-trained connectivity engineers of his generation did: working in relative institutional obscurity at companies that were quietly essential to every digital device on earth. He earned a BTech in electrical engineering from IIT Bombay, took an MS in EE at Stanford, and joined National Semiconductor in 1996, rising over sixteen years to Design Director before National Semiconductor's 2011 acquisition by Texas Instruments folded him into the acquiring company's product management organisation. By 2017 he was a Product Line Manager at TI — disciplined, margin-obsessed, process-driven — and he had spent long enough inside the largest analogue semiconductor company in the world to understand exactly what kind of company he did not want to build. In November 2017, Mohan co-founded Astera Labs with two colleagues from the same TI/NatSemi ecosystem.

Sanjay Gajendra, a year younger at 51, brought a complementary formation. His MEng in Engineering Management from Colorado-Boulder and an earlier stint as a principal software engineer at Wipro gave him an operational and systems-integration sensibility that was less common in design-led founding teams. He had rejoined the NatSemi orbit in 2006, moved to TI after the acquisition, and spent enough time in the intersection of India-US operational scaling and American product-line management to know how to run a supply chain and a go-to-market team simultaneously. From the company's first day he ran operations; in November 2023 the board formalised his expanded authority with the President title, making the Mohan-Gajendra pair the most visible leadership axis in Astera's public profile.

The third founding signature belongs to Casey Morrison, Astera's Chief Product Officer and the least publicly profiled of the three. Morrison owns the product strategy and roadmap — the architectural judgement that decided which interfaces to bet on (PCIe, CXL, Ethernet), which form factors to build retimers and fabric switches for, and when to expand adjacencies. That the product roadmap has proven so accurate in retrospect — Aries retimers became the margin engine of the AI rack, Leo memory controllers arrived at the CXL adoption inflection, Scorpio fabric switches positioned the company for the disaggregation thesis — is a material data point about Morrison's technical and market-timing instincts, even if the public record does not yet offer the biographical granularity of the CEO/COO pair.

## The executive layer rebuilt for scale

The FY2025 revenue number — $852.5 million at 75.7% GAAP gross margin — meant that by early 2026 Astera needed a CFO configured for a public company in operating at semiconductor-software-hybrid economics, not merely one capable of executing an IPO. [Mike Tate retired on March 2, 2026](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001736297), with transition services extended through September 1, 2026; his replacement was Desmond Lynch, who joined from Rambus Inc., where he had served as CFO since 2022 and VP Finance and Investor Relations since 2020. Lynch holds a BA in Accounting and Finance from the University of Glasgow and a Chartered Accountant designation from the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Scotland — a credential that signals balance-sheet rigour and treasury discipline more than deal-making optionality. His prior stops at Knowles, IDT/Renesas, and Atmel trace the mid-cap semiconductor P&L more completely than almost any CFO profile in the sector. The choice of a Rambus CFO — Rambus being the most IP-royalty-heavy balance sheet in US semiconductor mid-caps — carried an implicit signal: Astera's management was interested in how licensing and recurring-economics discipline could be applied as the product mix expanded.

Philip Mazzara, General Counsel since September 2022, completed the legal and corporate-governance stack. His JD/MBA from Stanford Law and the GSB, combined with five years running corporate-secretary and general-counsel functions at Innovium — the high-bandwidth switch-silicon company Marvell acquired in 2021 — gave him a precise understanding of how connectivity-silicon IP translates into litigation exposure, acquisition-process work, and SEC-compliance density. Innovium's arc from well-funded startup to Marvell acquisition was the most instructive single-company case study in connectivity-silicon M&A in the years before Astera's own IPO, and Mazzara had been inside it.

## Manuel Alba and the pattern-recognition chair

The chairman of the Astera board, Manuel Alba, turned 70 in the snapshot window and had sat in the chair since March 2018 — before the Series A closed, before the product roadmap had public confirmation, before the AI-rack buildout made connectivity retimers the highest-margin pickaxe of the cycle. His qualification for the seat was not financial-engineering expertise or operational CEO experience in the conventional sense; it was something rarer: a complete, personally executed map of how connectivity and compute-acceleration silicon companies get valued, acquired, and absorbed by the hyperscalers and system OEMs that dominate the AI-hardware supply chain.

Alba co-founded Galileo Technology in 1994, a switching-silicon company that Marvell acquired in 2001 and used as the architectural foundation for its networking product line. He then sat on the boards of Annapurna Labs through its acquisition by Amazon in 2015 — Annapurna became the design team behind AWS Nitro and Graviton — and Habana Labs through its acquisition by Intel in 2019, which became Intel's primary AI-training accelerator business. He has held board seats at Marvell itself, at Banias Labs, Lightbits, Xsight Labs, and Lyte.ai, among others. No other director at any AI-connectivity semiconductor company of comparable size carried as complete a set of personally observed connectivity-acquisition outcomes. For a company whose board was designed not around financial engineering but around architecture-cycle governance, Alba was the structural anchor.

## Craig Barratt and the Intel chairmanship overhang

The most consequential single board appointment of the eighteen months preceding the snapshot date was Craig Barratt, who joined in March 2025. The timing was not incidental. Barratt had spent the previous several months as the lead independent figure in Intel's board succession process; by November 2025 he was named an Intel director, and by March 2025 — concurrently with his Astera appointment — that succession work was reaching its terminal stage. On May 13, 2026, he was scheduled to assume the chairmanship of Intel Corporation, the most structurally significant seat in the American semiconductor industry.

Barratt's biography is the most densely connectivity-relevant on the Astera board after Alba's. He holds a PhD and MS in Electrical Engineering from Stanford and a BE in Electrical Engineering plus BS in Mathematics and Physics from the University of Sydney. He was President and CEO of Atheros Communications from 2003 to 2011, guiding it through the Wi-Fi connectivity buildout before Qualcomm acquired it; he then ran Qualcomm Atheros as President from 2011 to 2013. He took a turn as SVP of Google Access — the division responsible for Google Fiber and the company's infrastructure-access bets — from 2013 to 2017, then served as President and CEO of Barefoot Networks, the programmable-data-plane silicon company that Intel acquired in 2019. That acquisition put him inside Intel's Connectivity Group as SVP and General Manager from 2019 to 2020 before he departed to manage his public-company board portfolio, which has included Intuitive Surgical since 2011 and IonQ from 2021 to 2024.

The Intel chairmanship overhang is not a conflict in the regulatory sense — it was disclosed, the Astera audit committee has it — but it is a meaningful biographical fact about the information flows available to Astera's board in real time. Intel is both a foundry candidate, a memory-controller ecosystem participant, and a competitor-adjacent entity in the connectivity-silicon roadmap. Barratt's simultaneous presence at Astera's board table and Intel's chairman seat means that whatever architecture decisions Intel makes in PCIe and CXL ecosystem participation will pass through a single person who has observed Astera's product roadmap at director granularity. The Atheros overlap with Jack Lazar — who was CFO and Secretary at Atheros during the same years Barratt was CEO, and who also sits on the Astera board — is the most direct historical-working-relationship link among any two independent directors on the board. They executed one of the more consequential connectivity-silicon acquisitions of the previous decade together.

## The operating-CEO bench

Michael Hurlston, 59 and an Astera director since 2022, had accumulated a track record by the snapshot date that was genuinely unusual at his stage: he had been CEO of three public semiconductor companies in fewer than seven years. He ran Finisar — the optical transceiver manufacturer — from 2018 to 2019 before its merger with II-VI; ran Synaptics as President and CEO from 2019 to 2025; and assumed the President and CEO role at Lumentum Holdings in February 2025. He chairs Astera's Compensation Committee, which positions him to calibrate incentive structures for a management team navigating an architecture-transition cycle. The intersection of Lumentum's active-optical-transceiver business and Astera's Taurus smart cable module roadmap means Hurlston carries real-time read-through information about the AI-rack optical layer that almost no other independent director in the semiconductor space could match.

Stefan Dyckerhoff joined the board in 2019 as the institutional memory of the Series A process. As Managing Director at Sutter Hill Ventures since 2012, he led the investment that seeded Astera alongside his roles on the SiFive and Atmosic Technologies boards — both of which trace adjacent but distinct paths through the AI-era silicon buildout. His operating background at Juniper Networks, where he was EVP and General Manager in 2011-2012, and Cisco, where he ran VP/GM roles in 2007-2009, gave him system-architecture pattern recognition that translated into board contribution beyond the financial. He chairs Astera's Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. His former seat on the Enfabrica board (2020-2025) is the one item on the board's biographical map that requires careful framing: Enfabrica competed for adjacent AI-fabric territory, and Dyckerhoff's exit from that board in 2025 resolved the potential overlap cleanly before Astera's architecture bets became commercially consequential.

## The cross-industry breadth anchor

Bethany Mayer was appointed to the Astera board in June 2024, the most recent of the independent directors, and she arrived with the broadest simultaneous public-company footprint of any of them. At the snapshot date she held active director seats at Hewlett Packard Enterprise (since June 2023), LAM Research (since May 2019), and Box — where she was Chair (since April 2020). The DEF 14A designated her as the board's audit committee financial expert, a formal SEC determination that has specific accounting-literacy and financial-oversight implications. Her executive background ran from Apple and Cisco through Blue Coat Systems to HP's networking software and NFV divisions, before she served as President and CEO of Ixia from 2014 to 2017 — Ixia being the network-test and visibility company that Keysight acquired, whose core product set mapped directly onto Astera's connectivity-validation customer base. Her brief tenure at Sempra Energy in corporate development in 2018-2019 added a regulated-infrastructure perspective that none of the other independents carried. The combination of HPE (server OEM), LAM Research (semiconductor capital equipment), and Box (cloud-software governance) across a single director's active board portfolio gave Astera's governance a real-time read on the AI-server end market from three structurally different vantage points simultaneously.

Jack Lazar, Audit Committee Chair since December 2022, completed the financial oversight spine. His accounting degree from Santa Clara University anchored a career that ran from Atheros CFO — where he and Barratt executed the Qualcomm acquisition together — through SVP Corporate Development at Qualcomm itself, then to CFO of GoPro from 2014 to 2016 before independent consulting. His current board seats at GlobalFoundries (since July 2021), Resideo (since 2018), and Box (alongside Mayer) gave him foundry-cost pattern recognition — GlobalFoundries being one of the few advanced-node alternatives to TSMC that a US connectivity-silicon company might use — and a direct bilateral information channel with Mayer via the shared Box directorship.

## Compensation and incentive alignment

The [2025 proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001736297/000114036125015443/ny20044823x1_def14a.htm) disclosed that Mohan and Gajendra each carried a base salary of $615,000 and received cash bonuses of $1,332,725, driven by an annual incentive payout factor of 180.586% of target — a formula split 50/50 between revenue and non-GAAP operating margin achievement. Neither received new equity grants in 2025; the IPO-era awards from 2024 provided ongoing incentive alignment without creating additional dilution pressure. Non-employee directors received equity grants in the $200,000 to $210,000 range. The structure was consistent with a company that had already executed its public market entry, was generating GAAP net income of $219 million on $852.5 million of revenue, and was managing incentive design for the cycle-compression window rather than for the original-growth-story window.

The board that governed Astera at the snapshot date was not assembled for financial engineering or M&A optionality; it was assembled for architecture-transition governance. Three of the five independents — Alba, Hurlston, and Barratt — had personally led connectivity or accelerator silicon companies through full acquisition cycles. One was the Series A lead investor with Cisco and Juniper operating experience. One was the audit-grade CFO veteran with foundry and cloud-software read-through. One was the broadest cross-industry public-company director in the group. The absence of an investment-banking specialist was not a gap — it was a confirmation that the company was running on its operating model, not on deal optionality.
